questions.title: What does the cat say?
questions.prompt: A cat runs this script on a list called numbers. Read it carefully. Which sentence says what the cat says, for any list of numbers?

code.source:
when green flag clicked
set biggest to item 1 of numbers
for each n in numbers
    if n > biggest then
        set biggest to n
    end
end
say biggest

visual.alt: A friendly orange cartoon cat stands on a small wooden stage and looks up at an empty speech bubble.

source.prompt: An original friendly orange cartoon cat (not any existing character or mascot) standing on a small wooden stage, looking up, with an empty white speech bubble above its head. The speech bubble is completely empty. Style: flat vector illustration for 11-year-old students, simple rounded shapes, soft muted colours (sage green, warm cream, slate blue, a little mustard), a plain light cream background, no outlines heavier than needed. Absolutely no text, letters, numbers or symbols anywhere in the image. Landscape 4:3 composition with the subject centred and some empty space around it.

options: The first number in the list
The biggest number in the list
The last number in the list
How many numbers are in the list

followUp.prompt: For which list would the cat say 7?

glossary.note: The first thing in the list.
Runs the blocks inside once for every number in the list, with n standing for that number.
"Is greater than": n > biggest is true when n is bigger.

questions.details: Keeps the biggest number seen so far. The follow-up options set traps for students who think it says the first number (7, 9, 2) or the last one (9, 3, 7). Two marks for the description, one for the follow-up.

questions.title: Counting letters
questions.prompt: This script looks at every letter of a word. Which sentence says what it counts, for any word?

code.source:
set count to 0
for each letter in word
    if letter is a vowel then
        change count by 1
    end
end
say count

options: How many vowels are in the word
How many letters are in the word
Whether the word has a vowel in it (1 for yes, 0 for no)
How many letters in the word are not vowels

followUp.prompt: You want the script to count the letters that are not vowels instead. Which one line would you change?

glossary.note: One of the letters a, e, i, o or u.

questions.details: The if decides which letters are counted, so the change goes on line 3 ("if letter is not a vowel"). Changing line 4 changes how much is added, not which letters count.

questions.title: Putting items at the front
questions.prompt: These instructions build a new list called result from a list you give them. What do they show, for any list?

code.source:
set result to an empty list
for each item in the list, from first to last
    put item at the front of result
end
show result

options: The list sorted from smallest to largest
The list in the same order
The list in reverse order
Only the first item of the list

followUp.prompt: Which list would be shown exactly as it started?

glossary.note: Before everything already in result, so it becomes the new first item.

questions.details: Each item goes in front of the ones before it, so the last item ends up first. The follow-up asks which list reads the same backwards (2, 5, 2).

questions.title: Looking for a target
questions.prompt: Read this function. Which sentence says what find gives back, for any list and target?

code.source:
function find(list, target)
    set position to 1
    repeat while position ≤ length of list
        if item position of list = target then
            return position
        end
        change position by 1
    end
    return 0
end

options: How many items are equal to target
The position of the last item equal to target, or 0 if there is none
1 if target is in the list, 0 if it is not
The position of the first item equal to target, or 0 if there is none

glossary.note: The item at that position. Position 1 is the first item.
Stops the function straight away and gives back this value.

questions.details: A linear search that stops at the first match, because return leaves the function. The follow-up separates "returns 0" from "looks for 0": find([3, 0, 5], 0) gives 2.

questions.title: Tidying a list of words
questions.prompt: What does this Python function give back, for any list of words?
options: The words with repeats removed, each kept where it first appears
The words with repeats removed, each kept where it last appears
The words sorted into alphabetical order
Only the words that appear more than once

followUp.prompt: Which input gives back a list the same length as the input?

glossary.note: True when the value is nowhere in the list.
Adds an item to the end of a list.

questions.details: Removes duplicates and keeps first appearances in order: tidy(["b", "a", "b"]) is ["b", "a"]. Only a list with no repeats keeps its length.

questions.title: Checking the scores
questions.prompt: What does this Swift function tell you about a list of test scores?
options: true if at least one score is 50 or more
true if the first score is 50 or more
true only if every score is below 50
true only if every score is 50 or more

followUp.prompt: What does check([]) give back, for an empty list?
options: true
false
It crashes
nil

glossary.note: The function gives back true or false.
Leaves the function at once, giving back this value.

questions.details: Returns false at the first score below 50, so true means no score was below 50. With no scores the loop never runs and it returns true, which is the edge case the follow-up checks.

questions.title: The AI's top scorer
questions.prompt: You asked an AI assistant for a function that finds who scored the most. It wrote this. scores is a dictionary such as {"Ana": 12, "Bo": 9}. What does the code actually do?
options: Gives back the highest score itself, not a name
Gives back the name with the most points; if two tie, the one listed last
Gives back the name with the most points (the first listed if two tie), but None if nobody scored more than 0
Gives back the name with the most points for any scores, negative ones included

followUp.prompt: Which one line would you change so it also works when every score is negative?

glossary.note: Goes through the dictionary one name and its points at a time.

questions.details: The best-so-far starts at 0 instead of the first score, so all-negative (or all-zero) scores give None. > rather than >= keeps the first of a tie. Either line 3 (best = float("-inf")) or line 5 (if best_name is None or points > best:) fixes it on its own, so both earn the mark.

questions.title: Squashing text
questions.prompt: What does this Python function give back, for any text? For example, work out squash("aaba") first.
options: Each letter with how many times it appears anywhere in the text
Each run of the same letter in a row, written as the letter and the length of the run
The text with repeated letters removed
Each letter followed by its position in the text

followUp.prompt: Which input gives back text longer than the input?
options: "aaaa"
"aabb"
"abcd"
"aaab"

glossary.note: The letter at position i. The first letter is position 0.
Turns the number j - i into text, so it can be joined to a letter.

questions.details: Run-length encoding: "aaab" becomes "a3b1". The inner loop finds where each run ends. It only saves space when letters repeat, so "abcd" doubles in length.

questions.title: Explain it: shout
questions.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain what this Python function gives back for any list of names. Say what the result is, not what each line does.

rubric.description: Says it gives back a list of only the names with 3 or fewer letters, in capitals, and that longer names are left out.
Says only one of the two: that only short names are kept, or that the names are changed to capitals.
Describes something else, or retells the lines one by one without saying what the result is.

questions.details: A filter and a change in one loop: shout(["Ada", "Grace", "Bo"]) gives ["ADA", "BO"].

questions.title: Explain it: streak
questions.prompt: days has one true or false for each day, true if a habit was kept that day. In one or two sentences, explain what streak gives back, including when the habit was never kept. Say what the number means, not what each line does.

rubric.description: Says it gives back the longest run of days in a row where the habit was kept (the longest stretch of true values in a row), and 0 if there are none.
Says it gives back the longest run in a row but not what happens with no true values, or says it clearly but loosely ("the best streak").
Says it counts the days the habit was kept without saying they must be in a row, or describes current rather than best.
Describes something else, or retells the lines one by one without saying what the number means.

questions.details: current counts the run in progress and resets on a false; best keeps the largest current seen. [true, true, false, true] gives 2, not 3.
